extracted.intended_audience: nonprofit grant writers / development staff seeking foundation, corporate, or government funding
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance for preparing competitive grant proposals to foundations, corporations, and government funders, focused on common mistakes to avoid and application best practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not following instructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to follow the funder's stated application instructions (format, required documents, budget length, submission details).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foundations, corporations, and government agencies use instructions to sort professional applicants from amateurs. If the funder requires a three-year budget, provide one; if they request paper clips instead of staples, comply. Following directions is an easy-to-avoid but critical gatekeeping factor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failing to thoroughly research the funders’ interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Not researching and understanding a funder's specific interests and priorities (e.g., K–12 vs. adult education, focus on high-poverty schools).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Superficial research dooms many proposals. Read all of the foundation's guidelines and past grants to determine whether your project's purpose matches their specific priorities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focusing the proposal on the needs of your organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Centering the proposal on the nonprofit's internal needs (e.g., covering payroll or deficits) rather than on the funder's goals and beneficiary impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Frame requests in terms of the service delivered and outcomes for people served (e.g., ask for $10,000 to feed 7,000 people, not to cover a deficit). Even for operating support, explain how the grant enables you to do more for more people.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careless editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting text with typos, grammatical errors, or unclear sentences that force readers to re-read and lose confidence in the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use spell-check and grammar tools (e.g., Grammarly) and have someone else proofread. Well-edited proposals respect the reviewer’s time and appear more professional.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preaching to the choir
rubrics_metrics.description: Assuming the funder already knows about your organization or using jargon and catchphrases instead of clear explanations of capacity and plans.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Never assume prior knowledge; clearly describe your organization's ability to carry out the project. Use clear, simple language and avoid jargon so reviewers unfamiliar with your work can assess capacity and fit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not asking for the money
rubrics_metrics.description: Forgetting to state the specific dollar amount requested in the proposal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit—usually within the first sentence or two—about how much funding you are requesting. Reviewers cannot grant an amount you don't state.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asking for the wrong amount
rubrics_metrics.description: Requesting an amount that is substantially larger or smaller than the funder's typical grants or what they give to similar organizations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Research the sizes of past grants made to organizations like yours; many funders have preferred grant sizes. Asking for an atypical amount often results in rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting sloppy budgets
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing budgets that are incomplete, unreasonable, inconsistent with the narrative, or padded inappropriately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare the budget with as much care as the narrative; it should match the proposal point for point. Funders and program officers familiar with many budgets will spot missing line items, inflated salaries, or inconsistencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submitting a proposal late
rubrics_metrics.description: Failing to submit by the funder's deadline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Late submissions are perceived as amateurish and are easily avoidable; always meet deadlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not asking for a grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoiding submitting proposals because of perceived bad timing, busyness, lack of recognition by the funder, or other excuses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is rarely a 'perfect' time—economic downturns, busy schedules, or unfamiliarity with a funder are not valid reasons to avoid applying. Start researching and writing; you won't get funding if you don't try.
